title: Plans, wishes, and blessings
goal: Talk about what hasn't happened yet — plans, wishes, conditions, and blessings — including the set of greetings and good wishes you will need as soon as you have Javanese friends.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Rencana riyaya
dialogs.intro: Two weeks before Lebaran (Eid al-Fitr, the end of Ramadan). Rini is going home to Klaten; Dian doesn't know where she'll go yet. Pak Broto passes by and closes the conversation with a blessing — the most usual way to say goodbye in Java.

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Riyaya sésuk kowé arep nyang endi, Yan?
lines.id: Where are you going for Lebaran, Yan?
lines.literal: feast tomorrow you going-to to where, Yan?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Durung mesthi. Péngin mulih Jakarta, ning tikèté larang.
lines.id: Not sure yet. I'd like to go home to Jakarta, but the tickets are expensive.
lines.literal: not-yet certain. want go-home Jakarta, but ticket-the expensive.

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Nèk ora mulih, mèlu aku waé nyang Klaten.
lines.id: If you don't go home, just come with me to Klaten.
lines.literal: if not go-home, join me just to Klaten.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.id: Really? Won't it be any trouble?

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Ora babar pisan. Simbah malah seneng nèk ana tamu.
lines.id: Not at all. Grandma actually loves having guests.
lines.literal: not at all. grandma instead happy if exist guest.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Ya wis, tak pikir dhisik. Kapan mangkaté?
lines.id: OK, I'll think about it. When are you leaving?
lines.literal: yes already, I think first. when leaving-the?

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Bakal mangkat Setu ésuk, bèn ora kena macet.
lines.id: We'll leave Saturday morning, so we don't get stuck in traffic.
lines.literal: will leave Saturday morning, so-that not hit traffic-jam.

lines.speaker: Pak Broto:
lines.id: Going home for the holiday together, are you?

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Inggih, Pak. Kula badhé kondur Klaten.
lines.id: Yes, sir. I'm going home to Klaten.
lines.literal: yes, sir. I going-to go-home Klaten.

lines.speaker: Pak Broto:
lines.id: May your journey go smoothly. Take care.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Aamiin. Matur nuwun, Pak. Sugeng riyadi rumiyin.
lines.id: Amen. Thank you, sir. Happy Eid, in advance.
lines.literal: amen. thanks, sir. happy feast first.

notes: **Babar pisan** means "at all", and is almost always used with a negative: *ora babar pisan* (not at all). The krama is also *babar pisan*.
**Malah** means "on the contrary, actually". It reverses what the other person expected: *simbah malah seneng* (grandma would actually be pleased).
**Tak pikir dhisik** — "I'll think about it first". A polite and very common way to put off a decision; a flat refusal is rare in Java, and *tak pikir dhisik* gives both sides room.

**Kondur** is the krama inggil word for "to go home". Notice that Rini uses it **for herself** here — strictly speaking not quite right, but very common in real conversation, especially with words that have come to feel ordinary. You will hear many slips like this; they are no reason to worry.
**Lampah** means "way, journey, step" in krama. *Lampahipun lancar* = the journey goes smoothly. The word also appears in *lelampahan* (life experience).
**Sugeng riyadi** is "happy Eid" in Javanese. The full greeting: *Sugeng riyadi, nyuwun pangapunten lahir batos* — happy Eid, please forgive me, inside and out.

grammars.title: Four ways to talk about what hasn't happened yet
body: All four stand before the verb and don't change it at all. The difference is how certain it is and how much you want it.
after: **Arep versus péngin** is a distinction often mixed up. *Aku arep mulih* = I'm going home (decided). *Aku péngin mulih* = I'd like to go home (not sure I can). The dialogue above uses both in two consecutive sentences, and the difference shapes the whole conversation.
**Gelem is only for answering an invitation**, not for stating your own plan. *Kowé gelem melu?* — *Gelem.* Saying *aku gelem mulih* for "I'm going home" sounds odd.

grammars.title: Conditional sentences
body: The structure is just like English: the condition first, then the result — or the other way round; both are correct.

head: English
Ngoko
Krama
rows: If it rains, I won't go.
If you have time, drop by.
So as not to be late.

after: **Nèk** is the short form of *menawa* and by far the most common. Other forms with the same meaning: *yèn* (a little neater, common in writing) and *nek* (casual spelling).
**Bèn** and **supaya** both mean "so that". *Bèn* is far more common in conversation; *supaya* and its krama *supados* are more common in writing and in krama.

blocks.text: Javanese conversations often end with a blessing rather than "see you". This isn't a religious formality; it is the normal way to part, and not returning it feels cold. Two opening words take care of nearly everything: **muga-muga** (ngoko) and **mugi-mugi** (krama), "may…".

blocks.title: Sugeng tindak and sugeng kantun — a pair not to mix up
items: **Sugeng tindak** is said to **the person leaving**. **Sugeng kantun** is said to **the person staying**. Both are said at once when parting: the one leaving says *sugeng kantun*, the one staying replies *sugeng tindak*.
Swapping them makes your sentence mean the opposite, and it is the only mistake on this list that really sounds strange.
For everyday goodbyes, *mangga* and *ngatos-atos* (take care) are enough, and neither is ever wrong.

sections.title: Plans, the future, and declining gently

blocks.text: **Declining an invitation** is a skill that is more delicate in Java than in many places. A flat refusal — *ora* — is rarely given to anyone but close friends. Instead, people postpone or give a reason:

items: **Wah, kapan-kapan waé, ya.** — Oh, some other time, OK? A postponement everyone understands.
**Nuwun sèwu, kula wonten acara.** — Sorry, I have something on. A reason that needs no details.
**Tak pikir dhisik, ya.** — Let me think about it, OK? Puts off the decision without closing the door.
**Mbokmenawa mengko, nggih.** — Maybe later, OK? The gentlest of all.

blocks.title: Insya Allah, and what it means in Java
items: *Insya Allah* ("God willing") is widely used in Java, including by non-Muslims, and its meaning has drifted from the literal one. In everyday conversation it means **"probably yes, but no promise"**.
If you are invited and answer *insya Allah*, you haven't promised to come. If you invite someone and they answer *insya Allah*, don't count on the seat being filled.
This isn't dishonesty; it is a way of making sure no promise has to be broken. Javanese has many tools like this, and they all serve the same purpose: making sure nobody loses face.
Aku ____ mulih Jakarta, ning tikèté larang. (would like)
Aku ____ sinau basa Jawa nganti lancar. (would like)
Have a safe trip. (to the one leaving)

items: I get up at 5:00 every day.
I usually get home in the afternoon.
